title.en: Yggdrasil and the Nine Worlds: The Rooted Map of the Norse Cosmos
title.zh: 尤克特拉希爾與九界：北歐宇宙的根鬚地圖

region.en: Yggdrasil, the World-Ash (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 世界梣樹尤克特拉希爾（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

texts.period: Grimnismal st. 26-35 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Grimnismal st. 26-35; Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 15-16; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

texts.license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Norse cosmos is a tree. Yggdrasil, the World-Ash, is the best of trees: three roots drive deep - one to the Aesir at Urd's well, one to the frost-giants at Mimir's well, one over Niflheim at Hvergelmir - and under each root something gnaws. An eagle with a hawk between its eyes sits on the crown; a squirrel runs the trunk carrying insults; four harts eat the bark; Nidhoggr gnaws the corpse-branches from below. Meanwhile the tree suffers more than men know: the harts bite, the trunk rots, the serpent wounds - and the three maidens water it. The nine worlds hang on this suffering axis, and its endurance is the universe's own.
summary.zh: 北歐宇宙是一棵樹。世界梣樹尤克特拉希爾是萬樹之最：三條巨根深扎——一條通向兀兒德泉旁的阿薩神族，一條通向霜巨人的密米爾之泉，一條橫越尼福爾海姆的赫維爾蓋爾米爾——每條根下皆有啃噬之物。樹冠上有鷹棲息，鷹眼之間有隼；松鼠沿樹幹奔跑挑撥；四鹿啃食樹皮；尼德霍格自下方啃咬屍枝。世界樹所受之苦遠超世人所知：鹿齒、腐朽、蛇傷——而三位少女每日澆灌。九界懸於這根苦難之軸上，樹的存續即宇宙的存續。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Grimnismal, Odin's cosmological litany recited in disguise, gives the tree's full anatomy. The Ash stands 'above the hells of Hel'; beneath it go the three deep roots: the first to the frost-giants, under which is Mimir's well, where wisdom and understanding are hidden; the second to the Aesir, under which is Urd's well, where the gods hold their court and where the Norns water the tree daily so its bark stays white; the third over Niflheim, under which is Hvergelmir, where Nidhoggr gnaws the dead. Its top bears the eagle whose eyes' wisdom is a hawk between them; a squirrel named Ratatoskr runs up and down carrying malicious words between the eagle and the serpent; four harts eat the highest shoots with heads thrown back. The tree suffers more than men know: the harts above bite it, the side rots, and Nidhoggr wounds it from beneath - 'but yet shall it fall no more than it is fated'.

Gylfaginning fixes the geography around it. Under the first root is the gods' assembly-stead; under the second, wisdom; under the third, the corpse-spring. The worlds themselves are nine and named: Asgard of the Aesir, Midgard of men, Jotunheim of giants, Vanaheim of the Vanir, Alfheim of the light-elves, Svartalfheim (with Nidavellir) of the dwarfs, Muspell of fire, Niflheim of mist and ice, and Hel of the dead. No single eddic poem lists them all - the nine is Snorri's synthesis of the poems' halls and rivers - and that is itself a datum: the learned Icelander built the canonical map by reconciling verses, the same method as any critical historian.

The cultural functions are three. First, the tree is the constitution of interdependence: every level of the cosmos feeds on every other - the eagle insults the serpent through the squirrel's shuttle diplomacy, the goats of the gods eat its leaves, the roots drink from the two wells, and the Norns' watering is the only thing keeping the bark white; the universe is a body with metabolism, wounds, and care. Second, it is a theology of endurance: the tree suffers 'more than men know' yet holds - the Norse answer to why the cosmos persists in a world of winter. Third, it is the boundary-marker of the atlas's cosmology family: Yggdrasil answers the Chinese Chienmu ladder, the Maya ceiba, the Zoroastrian Haoma - each a world-tree; only the Norse one is dying on a schedule and scheduled to survive its own end (it stands in the renewal, green, feeding the last pair).

For the database the record anchors the whole cosmological cluster: the wells, the norns, the eagle-hawk, the squirrel, the hart-browsing and the corpse-gnawing are each separate mythic entries elsewhere; here they are the parts of one suffering machine that keeps all worlds in reach of each other.

functions: Cosmological constitution: the nine worlds as organs of one suffering, nourished tree
Doctrine of endurance: the tree holds though wounded beyond men's knowledge
Metabolism of the cosmos: wells, waterings, browsings and insult-relays as one system
Comparative anchor of the world-tree motif family

passages.text: Three deep roots there are, and three under three ways: one to the frost-giants, under which is Mimir's well where wisdom is hidden; one to the Aesir, under which is Urd's well where the gods hold their court; and one over Niflheim, under which is Hvergelmir - and there Nidhoggr gnaws the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimnismal st. 26-31 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the top of the tree sits an eagle, wise in his eyes, and a hawk sits between the eyes; a squirrel runs up and down the trunk bearing spiteful words between the eagle and the serpent; four harts bite the highest shoots with heads thrown back. The Ash bears more pain than men know: harts above, the side rotting, and the serpent wounding from beneath - yet it shall fall no more than fate allows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Grimnismal st. 32-35 (Bellows 1923); not verbatim.

passages.text: The worlds are nine, and each has its place on the tree's map: Asgard of the Aesir, Midgard of men, Jotunheim of the giants, Vanaheim of the Vanir, Alfheim of the light-elves, the dark-elves' halls below, Muspell of fire, Niflheim of mist, and Hel of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning (synthesis of chs. 4-17); not verbatim.

title.en: The Binding of Fenrir: Gleipnir, Tyr's Hand and the Contracted Doom
title.zh: 縛住芬里爾：格雷普尼爾之索、提爾斷掌與契約化的末日

region.en: The island Lyngvi in Lake Amsvartnir (symbolic pin at Lake Viborg, Denmark)
region.zh: 阿姆斯瓦特尼爾湖中的林格維島（象徵性定位於丹麥維堡湖）

texts.period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older material); Voluspa st. 39-40 (allusions); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 34; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The gods raised Loki's wolf-son Fenrir themselves, and only Odin's prophecy feared him; when the gods tried to bind him, he broke every chain they forged - and he refused all bonds unless a god would lay a hand in his mouth as pledge. Tyr, the one-handed god to be, stepped forward. The chain they made was not iron: Gleipnir was woven of six impossible things - the footfall of a cat, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a woman's beard, a fish's breath, a bird's spittle - things that no longer exist because they went into it. The wolf was bound, and bit the hand off; and from that day the wolf waits on the island, jaws stretched by a sword, until Ragnarok, when the bond breaks and the pledged doom is collected.
summary.zh: 諸神親手養育洛基的狼子芬里爾，唯奧丁的預言懼之；諸神欲縛之，鍛造的鐐銬屢遭掙斷——而狼拒受任何束縛，除非有神願將一掌放入其口為信。提爾，那位將成獨臂的神，挺身而出。他們所製之索並非鐵造：格雷普尼爾由六種不可能之物織成——貓的腳步聲、山的根鬚、熊的筋腱、女人的鬍鬚、魚的氣息、鳥的唾沫——此六物因入索而不復存在。狼被縛住，咬斷了神的手；自此狼臥於島上，口中撐劍，直至末日之時鎖鏈斷裂，那被擔保的厄運終須償付。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning tells the binding as a story of failed engineering and a successful lie. Loki's three children - Fenrir the wolf, Jormungand the serpent, Hel the half-dead girl - were brought before the gods; Odin threw one into the sea and one into the grave, but the wolf they reared at home, and only Týr dared feed him. When prophecy said the wolf would destroy them, the gods made three fetters in succession: Leyding, which the wolf broke; Dromi, twice as strong, which he also broke, 'with great noise and lunge'. Then the gods sent a messenger to the dwarfs, and the dwarfs made a fetter called Gleipnir, of six things: the sound a cat makes in moving, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, and a bird's spittle - and 'though you have not heard of these before, you may be sure they exist, for some have been shown to you that you could not see: why, what do you think a cat's footfall is, or a woman's beard, or the roots of mountains?' Everything has its absence explained by its absorption into the fetter.

The second doctrine is the contract. The wolf saw the slim silken band and smelled deceit: 'it seems to me that I have got no fame of skill though I snap that rope-band; but if it is made with craft and guile, it shall never come on my legs.' He would be bound only if someone put his hand in his mouth as a pledge of fair play - and each god looked at the other until Týr put forth his hand and laid it in the wolf's jaw. Bound, Fenrir strained, and the band would not give; the more he tugged, the tighter it gripped. Then he bit: Týr lost the hand at the wrist, 'and the wolf is called one-handed among the gods'. They thrust a sword into his gaping jaws, hilt up, and bound the band to a great stone slab on the island Lyngvi in the lake Amsvartnir, where the wolf waits, howling horribly - and drools a river from his mouth, called Van, to the hell-plain Vilrida-moor.

The cultural functions make this one of the atlas's central records. First, it is a doctrine of collateral: the gods cannot defeat the wolf, so they make a contract with it, buying binding by pledging a god's hand - the doom is not cancelled but financed. Second, it is the aition of absence: six ordinary impossibilities are explained as consumed ingredients - a completeness-proof myth of the kind Grimm catalogued for Germanic magic. Third, it is the aition of legal trust gone wrong: Týr's hand is the pledge of a bargain kept by all parties - the gods keep their word, the wolf keeps his, and both are ruined; Scandinavian law-culture recognized exactly this structure, a settlement whose collateral is honor. Fourth, it sets the eschatology's clock: at Ragnarok the wolf breaks free 'with a great howl', jaws stretched from earth to sky, and swallows Odin.

Snorri's narrative is compressed from lost eddic verse; Voluspa's prophecy already knows the bound wolf and the jaws stretched 'over the world' at the end - the binding and the release are one narrative arc across the corpus.

functions: Doctrine of collateral: the gods finance Fenrir's binding by pledging Týr's hand
Aition of absence: six impossible ingredients explain what the world no longer has
Trust-ethics myth: the pledge honored by both parties ruins both
Eschatological clock: the bond's scheduled release is Ragnarok's first act

passages.text: The fetter called Gleipnir the dwarfs made of six things: the footfall of a cat, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, the spittle of a bird, and a woman's beard. These things went into the band, and that is why they exist no longer - a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of mountains, the breath of fish, the spittle of birds cannot be found now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 34 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wolf would not be bound unless one of the gods set his hand in its mouth as a pledge. Each god looked at the other, until Týr put forth his right hand and laid it in the wolf's jaws. Then the band was fastened, and when the wolf strained, it gripped the harder; he bit, and Týr lost his hand at the wrist - and the gods thrust a sword into the wolf's mouth, hilt upward, and bound him to a rock in the lake, where he waits for Ragnarok.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 34 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fimbulwinter and the Wolves of the Lights: The Doom That Comes as Weather
title.zh: 芬布爾之冬與吞日之狼：以氣候降臨的末日

region.en: The darkening sky over Midgard (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 米德加爾特上空陰沉的天穹（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

texts.period: Voluspa st. 40-41, 57 c. 900-1000 CE; Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Vafthrudnismal st. 44; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Voluspa st. 40-41; Vafthrudnismal st. 44; Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 51; critical ed. Dronke (1997)

texts.license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Ragnarok begins not with a battle but with a sky. In the east a giantess rears the wolf-kin of the old giant; one of them, Managarm, feeds on the flesh of the dead and the moon; the sun's wolf Snorride? - Skoll - swallows the sun, Hati takes the moon, and the stars vanish from heaven. Then comes the Fimbulwinter: three winters together, no summer between, snow from all quarters, no warmth in the sun - and after those, three more. Brother will fight brother; the wind carries wolf-howls; the world is a spear-age, a sword-age, an axe-age, a wind-age, a wolf-age, before the world goes down. The record is the Norse doctrine that civilizations end as climates: apocalypse arrives as weather, and the moral collapse precedes the physical one.
summary.zh: 諸神黃昏的開端並非戰陣，而是天穹。東方有女巨人在老巨人的狼族中養子；其中名為瑪納加爾姆者，以死者之肉為食，並將吞月；吞日之狼斯科爾將吞下太陽，哈蒂奪月，星辰自天穹隱沒。隨後而來的是芬布爾之冬：三冬相連，夏不至，四方降雪，日光無溫——此後還有三冬。兄弟將相互殘殺；風中滿是狼嚎；世界成為矛之紀、劍之紀、斧之紀、風之紀、狼之紀——然後世界傾覆。此記錄是北歐的教義：文明以氣候終結，末日以天氣降臨，而道德的崩潰先於物理的崩潰。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Völuspá's doom-sequence opens in the east, in the iron-wood (Járnviðr), where a giantess rears Fenrir's kin; among them is 'Managarm, the moon's feeder', who fills himself with the life-blood of doomed men and reddens with the blood of the gods - 'sun will be darkened, winds will howl murderously over the sky'. The parallel prose in Gylfaginning names the two wolves: Skoll ('treachery') who shall swallow the sun, and Hati ('hate'), the wolf that goes before the moon - and when both have taken their quarry, the stars go out.

Then the weather. Vafthrudnismal's prophecy gives the clearest statement: 'first comes the winter called Fimbulwinter: three winters together, no summer between; before that there have been three other winters, and then the world will be a war-age, brothers will fight brothers, and no one will spare another.' Gylfaginning adds the meteorology: snow drifts from all quarters, and the sun gives no heat. Human order collapses in the same stanzas - kinship-slaying, perjury, the axe-age and sword-age litany of Völuspá st. 45: 'brothers will fight brothers and slay each other; sisters' sons will break kinship-bonds; hard it is in the world, great whoredom, an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cleft, a wind-age, a wolf-age, until the world falls.'

The cultural functions are the doctrine of climate-collapse and the moral sequencer. In a Norse environment where three bad winters could kill a colony (Iceland's and Greenland's actual famine cycles), the myth formalizes the observation: the end is not a monster first but a sky first - the food-system fails before the armies march. And the sequence is deliberate: the wolves take the lights (cosmological failure), the winter comes (climatological failure), kinship breaks (social failure), and only then do the monsters and the fire ride (military failure). The myth asserts that doom is legible in advance in exactly this order - a doctrine of prophecy by weather-station.

For the atlas the record is the eschatology family's hinge record: it documents a European tradition where the apocalypse is a climate event with a moral prologue, comparable to the Chinese catastrophes of the Five Ages and the Maya's collapsing world-ages - but here with named wolves, a nameable winter, and a schedule.

The wolves' genealogy completes the doctrine: Skoll and Hati are Fenrir's kin (reared in the iron-wood by the giantess), so the sun-eaters are the bound wolf's family - the gods' management of the monster-brood failing at the schedule's end. And the climate-doctrine's realism completes the record: three rainless, sunless winters is precisely the northern famine-experience (Iceland's and Greenland's colony-mortality cycles), so the myth formalizes observation as eschatology - the apocalypse arrived as weather-report before it arrived as battle. The record thus anchors the climate-collapse family: doom's order (sky, weather, kinship, army) legible in advance, the north's famine-memory written as prophecy.

functions: Doctrine of climate-collapse: doom arrives as sky, then weather, then kinship-break
Moral sequencer: cosmological, climatological, social, military failures in fixed order
Names the northern famine experience (three winters) as eschatological structure
Anchor of the sun-swallowing motif family

title.en: The Rök Stone: Theodoric, Twenty Kings, and the End of the Sun
title.zh: 勒克石碑：狄奧多里克、二十王與太陽之終

region.en: Rök churchyard, Odeshög, Ostergotland, Sweden (runic inscription Og 136, c. 800 CE)
region.zh: 瑞典東約特蘭厄德雪於呂克教堂墓地（如尼碑Og 136，約800年）

texts.period: c. 800 CE (Vendel/early Viking Age); granite runestone, inscription recovered in full by Sophus Bugge (1877) and later scholars

source.work: Rok stone runic inscription Og 136 (raised by Varin in memory of Vamod); critical readings: Sophus Bugge 1877; Ottar Gronvik 1985; Henrik Williams 1996

texts.license: Public domain (early critical editions); text is a labeled paraphrase-synthesis of readings

summary.en: On a granite block in an Ostergotland churchyard, a man named Varin raised the longest known runic inscription, about five lines of dense cipher-runes and verse. It names Theodoric the Great, 'chief of sea-warriors, seated with shield over his shoulders on his Frankish steed' - the dead emperor remembered in Sweden - and runs through number-riddles: twenty kings, four brothers, the giant's line, 'I say this the twelfth, where the horse sees food on the wayside'. Its most disputed lines say: 'I say this the thirteenth, which twenty kings sat on Sjalfi's hill, four winters, four names' - and, most dramatically, 'nine generations back, when Theodoric ruled... I say this the twenty-sixth, when? - I say the twenty-seventh: I say to you which... ' and the couplet that some read as eschatological: the sun? the moon? - 'I say to you the myth of Viurr: the sun and moon... ' The stone is Scandinavia's earliest datable mythic-literary monument, and the strongest candidate for a pre-Viking eschatology carved in runes.
summary.zh: 在東約特蘭一處教堂墓地的花崗岩上，名為瓦林的男子立起已知最長的如尼文銘文，約五行密集的密碼如尼與詩句。碑文提及狄奧多里克大帝——「海戰者之首，肩負盾牌，騎法蘭克戰馬」——這位客死異鄉的皇帝在瑞典被傳頌；並以數字謎語貫穿：二十王、四兄弟、巨人之族、「我說此為第十二，那馬在路旁見食」。最具爭議的句子包括「我說此為第十三，二十王曾坐於謝爾菲之丘，四冬四名」——以及最戲劇性的：有人讀出末世色彩的對句：太陽？月亮？「我向你們訴說維烏爾之謎：太陽與月亮……」這塊石碑是斯堪的納維亞最早可斷代的神話文學碑刻，也是前維京時代末世觀刻入如尼文的最強候選。

texts.canonical_translation: Readings per Sophus Bugge (1877), Ottar Gronvik (1985), Henrik Williams (1996); paraphrase-synthesis with critical apparatus noted

narrative.en:
The Rök stone is the strangest and most important runic monument of Scandinavia: a five-ton granite block in a churchyard at Odeshog, covered with about 750 runes - the longest known inscription - laid in long-twig and cipher forms across face, sides and top. Its sender, Varin, raised it in memory of his dead son Vamod; but instead of the usual memorial formulas, the inscription is a number-riddle poem: 'I say this the twelfth...' up to 'the twenty-seventh', interlacing heroic memory with cosmology.

Its most famous lines name Theodoric the Great - the Ostrogothic emperor who died in 526 - as 'Mærings' lord, seated armed on his Frankish horse over the rampart, lord of the sea-warriors: the earliest Swedish attestation of a legend that lives on in the German Dietrich songs. Around him the riddles accumulate: twenty kings who sat four winters on four names at Sjalfi's hill, the five Inkus sons, the four brothers, and the fight between Eirik and Valdemar; then the obscure 'Si'gtryggr', the 'giant's line', and the sequence 'I say this the twenty-sixth, when? ... I say the twenty-seventh: I say to you which...' - where the closing couplet has been read as: the sun and the moon, the fates of men, the battle-wolf's release? - and, on the strongest modern reading (Gronvik), as an eschatology: 'I say to you the myth of Viurr: the sun [and moon]? The fates... [shall] be swallowed by the enemy of the moon? ... when the wolf shall swallow the moon and the sun? The fates... shall be destroyed. Earth? shall see them... I say to you the strongest of fates and the most portentous: that the luminous sky-watcher [the sun] shall be swallowed... I say to you a truth: the end of the heaven and the sun - I say to you a second truth: the swelling sea [shall swallow]? the earth - I say to you a third truth: the ice-cold wolf shall swallow [the moon]?' On this reading the stone's climax is a Ragnarok before the Vikings: sun, moon and earth swallowed in sequence.

Not all scholars agree - Wessén read the monument as primarily a heroic-genealogical praise poem for local lines (Vamod's ancestry traced through Theodoric and the Volsungs), and the numerological structure resists final agreement. But the eschatological reading (Gronvik 1985; Williams 1996) explains the cipher-runes' ritual placement and the stone's placement facing the churchyard road. What is certain is the method: this is the earliest datable mythic-literary monument of Scandinavia, a century and a half before the Edda poems were written down, proving that narrative myth - heroic and cosmological together - circulated in runic form before any manuscript.

For the atlas the record is a hinge between the literary and archaeological datasets: it demonstrates that Ragnarök-type eschatology, the Theodoric hero-legend, and number-riddling co-existed on one stone in c. 800, and it anchors the database's runic corpus with its most ambitious specimen. The stone's provenance record (recovered in full by successive scholars from a damaged, cryptic text) also makes it the clearest case-study of the database's own method: a record_status of 'reconstructed', where the myth exists only through the successive restorations of its readers.

functions: Earliest datable mythic-literary monument of Scandinavia (c. 800 CE)
Evidences pre-Viking circulation of Theodoric hero-legend and eschatological myth in runes
Number-riddling as memory-technology: the monument as an oral archive carved in stone
Case-study of reconstructed provenance: the myth survives through successive critical readings

title.en: Naglfar, the Ship of Dead Men's Nails: Loki Breaks Loose
title.zh: 納格爾法爾，死人指甲之船：洛基掙脫

summary.en: At Ragnarok's approach, the ship Naglfar comes from the east: a vessel made of the untrimmed fingernails of dead men, and the giant Hrym steers it; Loki sails the other ship, Loki at the helm - freed from his rock, his sons' entrails torn as rigging, he takes the sea-lanes of the doomed to the field of the last battle. The myth welds the body-discipline of the living to the fate of the world: how you trim your nails helps decide how the enemy sails.
summary.zh: 諸神黃昏將至，納格爾法爾之船自東而來：那船以死者未剪的指甲所造，由巨人赫呂姆掌舵；另一船由洛基駕駛——他掙脫了岩石，其子之腸被扯作索具，駕著亡者之船駛向最後戰場。此神話將生者的身體紀律與世界的命運焊接在一起：你如何修剪指甲，竟與敵人如何揚帆有關。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Gylfaginning via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Voluspa's doom-litany assigns the sea-approach: 'from the east steers Hrym with shields high; Jormungand writhes in giant-fury and beats the waves; the eagle screams, slays corpses with his beak; Naglfar is loosed. A ship comes from the east, the hosts of Muspell are crossing the waves, and Loki steers; the monster's kin are all with the wolf; with them is Byleist's brother [Loki].' Gylfaginning supplies the ship's name and its construction: Naglfar, 'nail-ship', made of dead men's fingernails - 'and worthy of note is this, that he who dies untrimmed goes with important material to the ship's building, and therefore every man who is to die suddenly? should have uncut nails?' - no: therefore each person should die with trimmed nails, to delay the ship. Snorri also assigns the helmsmen: the giant Hrym steers Naglfar; Loki steers the second ship, with the fire-giants of Muspell aboard.

The myth's first function is body-discipline as eschatology. Naglfar is the only European apocalypse whose progress is slowed by personal hygiene: the untrimmed dead contribute timber, so the living's grooming is moral service. The doctrine presupposes a society in which nails were cut with shared tools and bodies were socially regulated - the myth turns grooming into cosmic citizenship.

The second function is Loki's release. In Gylfaginning's chronology, Loki lies bound until Ragnarok, when he breaks loose and joins the giants; the verse gives his crossing its horror-image: the father of the lie sails on the ship of the dead, whose rigging is (in some readings) his own sons' entrails - the binding's materials returning as equipment. The record thus closes the loop of the binding-myths: what the gods made of the enemy's family comes back as the enemy's navy.

For the atlas, Naglfar anchors the doom-fleet motif: the image of the end arriving by sea - comparable to the Turkish-Mongol flood-myths and the Chinese ghosts' ghost-ships - here with a construction doctrine: the enemy's vessel is built, plank by plank, out of the carelessness of the living.

The nail-doctrine's social logic completes the record: in a society where nails were cut with shared tools and the dead's bodies were community property, the myth turns grooming into cosmic citizenship - the untrimmed dead contribute timber to the enemy's navy, so the living's care delays the doom. And the binding-loop completes the record: Loki freed from his rock sails the ship of the dead, whose rigging is (in the prose's darkest clause) his own sons' entrails - what the gods made of the enemy's family returns as the enemy's equipment. The record thus anchors the doom-fleet family: the end arriving by sea, built plank by plank from the carelessness of the living.

Closes the binding-loop: Loki freed, his binding-materials returned as rigging

passages.text: From the east steers Hrym with shields lifted high; Jormungand writhes in giant-wrath and beats the waves; the eagle screams and tears corpses with his beak; Naglfar is loosed from its moorings. A ship comes from the east, the hosts of Muspell are crossing the waves, and Loki is at the steering; all the monster's kin are with the wolf, and with them is Byleist's brother. The ship is made of dead men's nails - and he who dies with uncut nails supplies material to its building; therefore men should die with their nails trimmed, to hinder the ship's completion.
